resulted in their formal description as the star spaces of all nontrivial 2-connected series-parallel graphs on $k + 1$ vertices and $n$ edges equipped with certain positive weights and arbitrary directions
Our computer experiments described in the next section allow us to suggest that in reality the equality holds, and it is achieved on a finite number of subspaces.

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract and introduction assert that the paper describes (characterizes) the class of subspaces deviating from every coordinate subspace by at least arccos(1/√n), i.e., that the extremal subspaces are exactly the star spaces of 2-sp-graphs with G-induced weights. The only formal result, Theorem thm:added-1, proves a single inclusion: every such star space deviates by at least arccos(1/√n). The reverse inclusion (every extremal/maximally deviating subspace arises this way) is proved nowhere; it rests solely on numerical experiments for n ≤ 9 and an OEIS count match, which the text itself phrases as suggestion. The stated characterization therefore exceeds the established content.

failure_location.quote: we describe the class of subspaces deviating from all the coordinate ones by at least $\arccos(1 / \sqrt{n})$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Weaken the prose: state that a family of such subspaces is constructed and that its exhaustiveness (finitely many extremal subspaces, parametrized by 2-sp-graphs) is a conjecture supported by the reported experiments.
issues.overall_effect: The informal framing overstates what is established: an unconditional construction of extremal-looking subspaces is presented as a description of the whole class. No labelled formal result is affected.
issues.title: Abstract/introduction claim to describe the whole class of extremal subspaces, but only one inclusion is proved
issues.why_classification: The repair is a local wording change that loses no proven content; every formal result and the experiments survive unchanged, only the unestablished characterization claim is dropped.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Graph-tree-induced edge coefficients are invariant to the choice of terminals up to a common factor.
We leave it as an exercise for the reader to prove the following property.
Let $G$ be a directed 2-sp-graph with vertices $l$ and $r$ treated as terminals, and $\tau$ be its spanning tree.
Our next step is to show that $Y_{\tau} y_{\tau} = \frac{1}{n} y_{\tau}$, where $y_\tau$ is the restriction of the vector of $(G,\tau)$-induced coefficients to the set of $\tau$'s edges.

issues.failure_explanation: The (G,τ)-induced coefficients are defined relative to a chosen terminal pair (their definition begins 'Let G be a directed 2-sp-graph with vertices l and r treated as terminals'). The proof of the eigenvalue equation Y_τ y_τ = (1/n) y_τ treats each row e0 separately, re-choosing the terminals as e0's endpoints and re-orienting all edges from l to r; the decomposition, the weight/coefficient chains, and the recursions (rec4)-(PP) all use this per-row choice. As written, the computation therefore produces a different candidate vector y for each row e0. These per-row vectors coincide up to a common factor — and hence form a single eigenvector — only by Proposition prop:added-1, which the paper states but explicitly leaves unproved. The proof of the main theorem thus relies on an unestablished premise and is incomplete as written.

failure_location.quote: Let us denote $e_0$'s vertices by $l$ and $r$ and treat them as the terminals.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply a proof of Proposition prop:added-1 — e.g., by adapting the decomposition-tree rerooting argument given for Proposition prw to the ψ-coefficients with their tree/forest sign cases — and invoke it explicitly to identify the per-row vectors with one fixed eigenvector.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem thm:added-1 lacks a complete proof; Corollary cor:added-1 (the √n estimate in the Hypothesis cannot be improved for any n and k) inherits the gap, as do the prose claims about the extremal subspaces.
issues.title: Main theorem's proof needs terminal-independence of the (G,τ)-coefficients, which is stated but explicitly unproven
issues.why_classification: No statement needs to be weakened and the missing argument is contained (a sibling statement is fully proved in the paper), but the repair requires writing a genuine lemma-level proof on which the main theorem's eigenvector conclusion depends — more than a local routine fix, less than new proof architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In all the experiments we have conducted for various $n$ and $k$, this value was equal to $\arccos(1 / \sqrt{n})$.
\State \text{Print( "The hypothesis is solved in negative" )} \Comment{(Never seen this)}

issues.failure_explanation: d = Distance(A) is the target function measuring the least deviation from the coordinate subspaces, i.e., an angle: the text states that its greatest observed value equals arccos(1/√n). The algorithm instead compares d with the cosine 1/sqrt(n) ± ε. Since arccos(1/√n) > 1/√n for every n ≥ 2 (e.g., n = 2: π/4 ≈ 0.785 > 1/√2 ≈ 0.707), every extremal subspace satisfies d > 1/√n + ε for small ε and enters the first branch, printing 'The hypothesis is solved in negative' and returning −1 — contradicting the annotation '(Never seen this)' and the fact that the experiments accumulated nonempty sets ES. Symmetrically, the ElsIf test d > 1/√n − ε accepts any subspace whose deviation lies between 1/√n and arccos(1/√n), so ES would contain non-extremal subspaces. With mismatched units the procedure cannot deliver its stated output ('a set of extremal subspaces ES').
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Make the units consistent: compare d with arccos(1/sqrt(n)) ± ε (equivalently, compare cos d against 1/√n ∓ ε).
issues.overall_effect: The appendix pseudocode underlying the reported experiments is incorrect as written: it would abort on the first extremal subspace found and never build the set ES whose symmetry classes are counted in Table tab. No formal result depends on it.
issues.title: Extremal-subspace search algorithm compares an angle-valued target function against the cosine threshold 1/sqrt(n)
issues.why_classification: A single forced local correction to the pseudocode's thresholds restores the described behavior; the experiments, tables, and all substantive mathematical claims survive unchanged.
